frq.question:
Consider the cardioid r = 1 + cos θ.
(a) Write the parametric components x(θ), y(θ) and compute dx/dθ and dy/dθ.
(b) Find all θ in [0, 2π) giving horizontal tangents, and the corresponding points.
(c) The angle θ = π zeroes both component derivatives. Use the pole-tangent rule to give the tangent line there anyway.
rubric: (a) x = (1 + cos θ)cos θ, y = (1 + cos θ)sin θ; dy/dθ = (2cos θ - 1)(cos θ + 1), dx/dθ = -sin θ(1 + 2cos θ)
(b) cos θ = 1/2: θ = π/3, 5π/3 (cos θ = -1 is the both-zero flag); points (3/4, ±3√3/4)
(c) r = 0 at θ = π: tangent is the line θ = π (the x-axis)
Both-zero angle handled by the rule, not forced into a list
frq.model_answer: (a) x(θ) = (1 + cos θ)cos θ, y(θ) = (1 + cos θ)sin θ. Product rule: dy/dθ = -sin θ·sin θ + (1 + cos θ)cos θ = cos θ + cos²θ - sin²θ = 2cos²θ + cos θ - 1 = (2cos θ - 1)(cos θ + 1). dx/dθ = -sin θ·cos θ - (1 + cos θ)sin θ = -sin θ(1 + 2cos θ). (b) dy/dθ = 0 at cos θ = 1/2 (θ = π/3, 5π/3) and cos θ = -1 (θ = π). At π/3 and 5π/3, dx/dθ = -sin θ(2) ≠ 0: genuine horizontal tangents. There r = 3/2, giving points (3/2·cos(π/3), 3/2·sin(±π/3)) = (3/4, ±3√3/4). (c) θ = π zeroes both derivatives — the cusp. But r(π) = 0: by the pole-tangent rule the curve enters the origin tangent to the line θ = π, i.e., the x-axis. The heart's point sits on the axis it aims along.

frq.question:
Consider the limaçon r = 1 + 2cos θ.
(a) Find the tangent lines to the curve at the pole.
(b) Determine whether the curve's distance from the origin is increasing or decreasing at θ = π/6, with the one-sentence justification.
(c) Find the slope dy/dx at θ = π/2.
rubric: (a) r = 0 at θ = 2π/3, 4π/3: tangents are those two lines through the origin
(b) dr/dθ = -2sin(π/6) = -1 < 0: distance decreasing
Components rebuilt by product rule
frq.model_answer: (a) 1 + 2cos θ = 0 at θ = 2π/3 and 4π/3. By the pole-tangent rule, the curve crosses the origin twice, tangent to the lines θ = 2π/3 and θ = 4π/3 — the inner loop's two edges. (b) dr/dθ = -2 sin θ; at π/6: -1 < 0, so the curve's distance from the origin is DECREASING at that sweep moment. (c) At θ = π/2: r = 1, dr/dθ = -2. dy/dθ = r'sin θ + r cos θ = -2(1) + 1(0) = -2. dx/dθ = r'cos θ - r sin θ = -2(0) - 1(1) = -1. Slope = (-2)/(-1) = 2 — the curve climbs at slope 2 as it crosses the point (0, 1).

frq.question:
A bug walks the spiral r = θ for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π (θ in radians, r in cm).
(a) Explain — without computing any quotient — why the bug's distance from the pole is increasing for the entire walk.
(b) Compute the slope dy/dx at θ = π/2 and interpret the tangent direction.
(c) Set up (do not evaluate) the arc length integral for the full walk, using the polar arc length form √(r² + (dr/dθ)²).
rubric: (a) dr/dθ = 1 > 0 throughout: the radial dial is always positive
(b) At π/2: x = θcos θ, y = θ sin θ: dy/dθ = sin θ + θcos θ = 1; dx/dθ = cos θ - θ sin θ = -π/2: slope = -2/π
Interpretation: at the top of the first turn the spiral heads up-and-left, gently
frq.model_answer: (a) dr/dθ = 1, positive for every θ: at each sweep instant the bug's radius grows — the spiral unwinds outward monotonically, no quotient needed. (b) Components x = θ cos θ, y = θ sin θ: dy/dθ = sin θ + θ cos θ, dx/dθ = cos θ - θ sin θ. At θ = π/2: dy/dθ = 1 + 0 = 1; dx/dθ = 0 - π/2 = -π/2. Slope = 1/(-π/2) = -2/π ≈ -0.64. At the point (0, π/2) — directly above the pole — the tangent slopes gently downward to the right, meaning the spiral is cresting: moving leftward across the top of its first turn while its height begins to ease. (c) With r = θ and dr/dθ = 1: L = ∫₀^{2π} √(θ² + 1) dθ — the polar arc length form, complete as a setup.

hook: Rectangles can't tile a pie slice — but sectors can. Polar area swaps Unit 6's rectangle slices for infinitesimal pie wedges: A = (1/2)∫r² dθ. One new formula, the unit's old discipline, and the BC exam's final geometry question falls.
learning_objectives: Derive and apply the polar area formula A = (1/2)∫r² dθ
Choose integration bounds from the sweep that traces the region once

Combine symmetry, identities, and the calculator per the section's rules

sections.title: Sectors, Not Rectangles
sections.subtitle: Deriving (1/2)∫r² dθ
sections.body:
A thin polar slice — the region swept between angles θ and θ + dθ — is approximately a circular SECTOR of radius r and angle dθ: area (1/2)r² dθ (the circle-fraction formula: (dθ/2π)·πr²). Summing wedges across the sweep: A = (1/2)∫ₐᵇ r² dθ. The slicing habit of Unit 6, with wedges where rectangles were — chop, measure a piece, sum, one more time.

Sanity anchor: the full circle r = R over [0, 2π]: (1/2)∫₀^{2π} R² dθ = (1/2)R²(2π) = πR² ✓. The formula re-derives the area it generalizes, as every slicing formula has.

Worked: the cardioid r = 1 + cos θ. Full area: (1/2)∫₀^{2π} (1 + cos θ)² dθ = (1/2)∫₀^{2π} (1 + 2cos θ + cos²θ) dθ. Over the full period: the middle term dies, cos² contributes π (the half-angle identity cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2): A = (1/2)(2π + 0 + π) = 3π/2. The cos²-integrates-to-half-the-interval pattern is polar area's recurring arithmetic — internalize ∫₀^{2π} cos²θ dθ = π and its sin twin.

The squared radius is the formula's tested detail: A involves r², so the integrand is the WHOLE radius expression squared — (1 + cos θ)², binomial expansion and all. Forgetting the square, or squaring termwise, are the founding errors; the expansion-then-identity workflow is the antidote.
key_terms: A = (1/2)∫r² dθ: sector slices summed across the sweep
cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2: ∫ over a full period gives half the length
(1 + cos θ)² expands fully — the binomial is the integrand
boxes: ap_alert

The 1/2 out front and the SQUARE on r are both graded and both droppable under pressure: write A = (1/2)∫ᵅᵝ [whole r expression]² dθ as a template line before substituting anything. The template is the antidote to the genre's two founding errors.

sections.title: Bounds from the Sweep
sections.subtitle: Trace once, integrate once
sections.body:
Polar area bounds are ANGLES, chosen so the sweep traces the region exactly once. The full cardioid: 0 to 2π. A petal of r = 2cos(3θ): the r = 0 bounds — cos(3θ) = 0 gives 3θ = ±π/2: θ from -π/6 to π/6 — one petal swept once. Chapter 6's pole-passage solve IS the bounds question; the area integral just inherits it.

The petal computation, completed: A = (1/2)∫_{-π/6}^{π/6} 4cos²(3θ) dθ = ∫_{-π/6}^{π/6} (1 + cos 6θ) dθ = [θ + sin(6θ)/6] = (π/6 + 0) - (-π/6 + 0) = π/3. All three petals: π. The total-flower shortcut — one petal times the count — beats any blind full sweep, because how 0-to-2π covers a rose depends on its parity: odd-n roses are traced exactly once, while even-n roses draw their 2n petals from a mix of positive- and negative-r stretches that takes care to audit. The safe universal play: compute ONE petal from its r = 0 bounds, multiply by the petal count.

The inner loop of r = 1 + 2cos θ: bounds are its pole-passages, 2π/3 to 4π/3 — the sweep where r ≤ 0, whose squared values trace the small loop. The square erases the sign: the formula integrates r² regardless, and the loop's area is (1/2)∫_{2π/3}^{4π/3} (1 + 2cos θ)² dθ = π - (3√3)/2 after the expansion-identity grind.

Double-counting is the genre's silent killer, and the defense is visual: SKETCH the region, mark the sweep's start and end angles on the sketch, and confirm the radius arm crosses the region once. Thirty seconds of geometry before any integration — the polar edition of Unit 8's sketch-first discipline.
key_terms: Chosen so the radius arm sweeps the region exactly once
Petal bounds from r = 0; multiply by n — the rose-proof play
Negative-r stretches integrate correctly: r² doesn't care
boxes: ap_alert
Rose areas: NEVER integrate 0 to 2π blind — even-n roses double-trace. One petal from its r = 0 bounds, times the petal count, is correct for every rose and is the expected work.

sections.title: Between Two Curves
sections.subtitle: Washers go polar
sections.body:
The region between an outer polar curve R(θ) and an inner r(θ), over a shared sweep: A = (1/2)∫ₐᵇ (R² - r²) dθ — outer squared minus inner squared, the washer logic in wedge form. The same cardinal error lurks: (R - r)² is NOT R² - r²; the squares subtract individually, exactly as in Unit 8's revolution washers.

The standard configuration: 'the region inside the circle r = 3cos θ and outside the cardioid r = 1 + cos θ.' Bounds from the intersections (chapter 6's solve): cos θ = 1/2, θ = ±π/3 — between them the circle rides outside. A = (1/2)∫_{-π/3}^{π/3} [9cos²θ - (1 + cos θ)²] dθ. Expansion, identities, symmetry (even integrand: 2∫₀^{π/3}): the grind is routine once the setup stands; the setup is the intersection solve plus the outer/inner identification.

Who's outside: test ONE angle inside the sweep (θ = 0: circle 3 versus cardioid 2 — circle outside ✓), the polar twin of area-between-curves' order check. When curves trade outsideness mid-region, split at the crossing angles — trading places is as real in wedges as it was in slices.

'Inside both curves' regions (the lens between the circle and cardioid) decompose by sweep: from each angle, the NEARER boundary caps the wedge — typically the region splits at the intersection angles into pieces each governed by one curve. Sketch, identify which curve bounds each angular stretch, sum the pieces: (1/2)∫(cardioid²) over its stretch plus (1/2)∫(circle²) over the rest. The decomposition mirrors Unit 8's compound regions, wedge edition.
key_terms: (1/2)∫(R² - r²) dθ: outer square minus inner square, per wedge
One angle inside the sweep settles which curve is outer
Split at intersections; each stretch keeps its nearer boundary
boxes: ap_alert

Between-curves bounds come from the FULL intersection protocol — including the pole check. A missed origin-intersection truncates the sweep and silently halves regions; the chapter-6 protocol is the area question's first graded step.

sections.title: The Polar Battery and the Unit's Close
sections.subtitle: Exam form, and what carries forward
sections.body:
The polar FRQ's standard anatomy: (a) sketch or identify the curves; (b) find intersections (with the pole check); (c) compute an area — petal, loop, between, or inside-both; (d) a derivative item — dr/dθ interpretation or a tangent. Parts (b) and (c) carry the weight; chapter 6's protocol and this chapter's template are their respective rubrics.

Calculator division of labor: polar areas on active sections evaluate numerically — the setup (template, bounds, squared expressions) is the human work, with cos²-identity grinds outsourced. No-calculator polar areas keep the trig arithmetic tame (full periods, symmetric bounds) and expect the identity workflow by hand. Both sections grade the template line.

The unit's tools, final census: parametric trips and their slopes, speeds, lengths; vector packaging; planar motion's six-question battery; polar addresses, garden, derivatives, areas. One thread ran through: componentize or reparametrize, then apply the old calculus. Nothing in the unit was new mathematics — it was new GEOMETRY for the same derivatives and integrals, which is exactly how to retain it.

What remains: Unit 10 — infinite series, BC's capstone. Different in flavor (sums, not slices), it still leans on this course's spine: improper-integral convergence (Unit 6), the derivative tower (Units 2-3) for Taylor coefficients, and error-bounding instincts from every approximation chapter. The road geometry is done; the last unit counts forever.

(1/2)∫(...)² dθ with bounds: the human work both sections grade
Reparametrize, then run the old calculus — no new mathematics

Polar area answers on calculator sections: write the template with bounds and squared radii, then the three-decimal value. The identity grind is OPTIONAL there — the machine integrates cos² happily — but the visible setup is not.

Let R be the region enclosed by one petal of the rose r = 4 sin(2θ).
(a) Find the bounds of the petal lying in the first quadrant.
(b) Compute the petal's area exactly.

(b) A = (1/2)∫₀^{π/2} 16 sin²(2θ) dθ = 4∫₀^{π/2} (1 - cos 4θ) dθ = 4[θ - sin(4θ)/4]₀^{π/2} = 4(π/2) = 2π. (c) Total area: four congruent petals give 4 × 2π = 8π. A blind 0-to-2π integral is risky in general because it requires knowing exactly how the sweep covers the flower — even-n roses draw half their petals from negative-r stretches, and miscounting coverage silently doubles or halves regions. (For this curve the full sweep does trace each petal once, and (1/2)∫₀^{2π} 16 sin²(2θ) dθ = 8π agrees — but the per-petal route never needed that audit.)

frq.question:
Let R be the region inside the circle r = 3 cos θ and outside the cardioid r = 1 + cos θ.
(a) Find the intersection angles bounding R, including the pole analysis.
(b) Verify which curve is outer on the sweep, and write the area integral.
(c) Evaluate the area exactly.
rubric: (a) 3cos θ = 1 + cos θ: cos θ = 1/2, θ = ±π/3; pole: both curves reach r = 0 (at π/2 and π) but the region between ±π/3 doesn't involve the pole crossing
(b) At θ = 0: circle 3 > cardioid 2: circle outer; A = (1/2)∫_{-π/3}^{π/3}[9cos²θ - (1+cos θ)²]dθ
(c) Expand: 8cos²θ - 2cos θ - 1; integrate: 8(θ/2 + sin2θ/4) - 2sin θ - θ → evaluates to π
Symmetry (2∫₀^{π/3}) and identity work shown; exact answer π
frq.model_answer: (a) Setting 3 cos θ = 1 + cos θ: cos θ = 1/2, θ = ±π/3 — the lens's corners at (3/2, ±π/3). (Both curves separately visit the pole — the circle at π/2, the cardioid at π — so the origin is an intersection of the curves, but it does not bound THIS region, which lives in the sweep |θ| ≤ π/3.) (b) Test θ = 0: circle r = 3 versus cardioid r = 2 — the circle rides outside. A = (1/2)∫_{-π/3}^{π/3} [9cos²θ - (1 + cos θ)²] dθ. (c) Expand the integrand: 9cos²θ - 1 - 2cos θ - cos²θ = 8cos²θ - 2cos θ - 1 = 4(1 + cos 2θ) - 2cos θ - 1 = 3 + 4cos 2θ - 2cos θ. An antiderivative of 3 + 4cos 2θ - 2cos θ is 3θ + 2 sin 2θ - 2 sin θ. By evenness the symmetric evaluation doubles the half-range and cancels the leading 1/2: A = [3θ + 2 sin 2θ - 2 sin θ]₀^{π/3} = π + 2(√3/2) - 2(√3/2) = π. The lens-complement's area is exactly π.

(b) A = (1/2)∫₀^{2π}(2 + sin 3θ)² dθ = (1/2)(8π + 0 + π) = 9π/2 ≈ 14.137 (exact possible: 4 + sin² average)

(b) The curve closes over one full sweep: A = (1/2)∫₀^{2π} (2 + sin 3θ)² dθ = (1/2)∫₀^{2π} (4 + 4 sin 3θ + sin²3θ) dθ = (1/2)(8π + 0 + π) = 9π/2 ≈ 14.137. (The middle term dies over full periods; sin² contributes half the interval.) (c) dr/dθ = 3 cos(3θ); at θ = π/4: 3 cos(3π/4) = -3√2/2 ≈ -2.121. Negative: at that sweep moment the curve is moving TOWARD the pole — the ring is in one of its three inward-breathing phases.
